traditional-jazz.album: The Hot Fives and Hot Sevens, Vol. 1
traditional-jazz.note: A landmark series of recordings that introduced individual improvised solos into New Orleans jazz, which had been built on collective improvisation. These sessions shaped the vocabulary of jazz for decades to come.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Louis Armstrong (tp, vo), Johnny Dodds (cl), Kid Ory (tb), Lil Armstrong (p), Johnny St. Cyr (banjo)

traditional-jazz.note: A monumental early-jazz recording from Chicago featuring a young Louis Armstrong. Captures the polyphonic beauty of collective improvisation at its source.
traditional-jazz.personnel: King Oliver (cornet), Louis Armstrong (cornet), Johnny Dodds (cl), Honore Dutrey (tb), Lil Hardin (p), Bill Johnson (banjo, b), Baby Dodds (ds)

traditional-jazz.artist: Jelly Roll Morton and His Red Hot Peppers
traditional-jazz.album: Jelly Roll Morton and His Red Hot Peppers
traditional-jazz.note: An ensemble led by the composer who called himself "the inventor of jazz." Balancing improvisation with meticulous arrangement, this group anticipated the swing era to come.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Jelly Roll Morton (p), George Mitchell (tp), Kid Ory (tb), Omer Simeon (cl), Johnny St. Cyr (banjo), John Lindsay (b), Andrew Hilaire (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: Recordings by the virtuoso who established the soprano saxophone as a vehicle for jazz expression, marked by blues-derived, keening phrasing.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Sidney Bechet (ss, cl), Sidney De Paris (tp), Vic Dickenson (tb), Art Hodes (p), Pops Foster (b), Manzie Johnson (ds)

traditional-jazz.album: Bunk Johnson and His Superior Jazz Band
traditional-jazz.note: A trumpeter who had stepped away from music was rediscovered amid the New Orleans jazz revival, documented here. His raw, powerful playing became a touchstone of the revivalist movement.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Bunk Johnson (tp), George Lewis (cl), Jim Robinson (tb), Walter Decou (p), Lawrence Marrero (banjo), Alcide Pavageau (b), Ernest Rogers (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: Recordings by the trombonist who established the exuberant tailgate style. Ory was a central figure in the West Coast revival of New Orleans jazz.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Kid Ory (tb), Mutt Carey (tp), Omer Simeon (cl), Buster Wilson (p), Bud Scott (banjo, g), Ed Garland (b), Alton Redd (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: Jam-session recordings in the Chicago style, assembled by the guitarist and scene-fixer Condon. Favors momentum and conversational give-and-take over formal arrangement.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Eddie Condon (g), Wild Bill Davison (cornet), Cutty Cutshall (tb), Bud Freeman (ts), Gene Schroeder (p), Leonard Gaskin (b), George Wettling (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: Recordings whose elegant, songful cornet solos left a deep mark on later generations. Beiderbecke's pursuit of tonal beauty over raw power set him apart from his peers.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Bix Beiderbecke (cornet), Frankie Trumbauer (C-melody sax), Bill Rank (tb), Jimmy Dorsey (cl, as), Itzy Riskin (p), Howdy Quicksell (banjo), Chauncey Morehouse (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: A defining session by a Chicago-school player whose playing retained a strong ragtime-derived rhythmic feel. His full-bodied cornet tone helped sustain the Dixieland revival.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Muggsy Spanier (cornet), George Brunies (tb), Rod Cless (cl), Ray McKinstry (ts), Joe Bushkin (p), Bob Casey (b), George Wettling (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: Often cited as the first commercial jazz recording. Its animal-call effects and other novelty touches make it a valuable document of early jazz's entertainment appeal.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Nick LaRocca (cornet), Larry Shields (cl), Eddie Edwards (tb), Henry Ragas (p), Tony Sbarbaro (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: An ensemble led by the clarinetist whose smooth tone graced Chicago's club scene. Its sophisticated harmonic sense foreshadowed the coming swing era.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Jimmie Noone (cl), Joe Poston (as), Earl Hines (p), Bud Scott (banjo, g), Johnny Wells (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: A rich live recording from the formation of the All Stars. Armstrong moved from big-band format back to a small group, reaffirming the spirit of early jazz.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Louis Armstrong (tp, vo), Jack Teagarden (tb, vo), Barney Bigard (cl), Dick Cary (p), Bob Haggart (b), Sid Catlett (ds), Velma Middleton (vo)

traditional-jazz.note: A band recording led by the trombonist who drove San Francisco's revivalist scene. Combines fidelity to traditional style with raw, visceral energy.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Turk Murphy (tb), Bob Scobey (tp), Bob Helm (cl), Burt Bales (p), Harry Mordecai (banjo), Pat Patton (b), Bill Dart (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: A striking record from a clarinetist raised in New Orleans, marked by a simple, almost prayerful tone. Lewis became an emblematic figure of the revival boom.
traditional-jazz.personnel: George Lewis (cl), Kid Howard (tp), Jim Robinson (tb), Alton Purnell (p), Lawrence Marrero (banjo), Alcide Pavageau (b), Joe Watkins (ds)

traditional-jazz.note: A band that deliberately turned its back on the swing craze to return to traditional New Orleans style. The starting point of the West Coast Dixieland revival.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Lu Watters (tp), Bob Scobey (tp), Turk Murphy (tb), Bob Helm (cl), Wally Rose (p), Clancy Hayes (banjo, vo), Dick Lammi (tuba, b), Bill Dart (ds)

traditional-jazz.album: Papa Celestin and His Tuxedo Jazz Band
traditional-jazz.note: Recordings by a veteran bandleader who never left New Orleans. A valuable document of the living style kept alive by musicians who stayed in the city.
traditional-jazz.personnel: Papa Celestin (tp), Alphonse Picou (cl), Bill Matthews (tb), Jeanette Kimball (p), Manuel Crusto (b), Josiah Frazier (ds)

swing.note: The pinnacle of the Basie band's sophisticated big-band arrangements and razor-tight rhythm section unity. A defining statement of Basie's swing feel.
swing.personnel: Count Basie (p), Thad Jones, Wendell Culley, Snooky Young (tp), Henry Coker, Al Grey, Benny Powell (tb), Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Frank Foster, Charlie Fowlkes (sax), Freddie Green (g), Eddie Jones (b), Sonny Payne (ds)

swing.note: The legendary live album that revived Ellington's band during a career slump. Paul Gonsalves's marathon tenor solo drove the crowd into a frenzy.
swing.personnel: Duke Ellington (p), Cat Anderson, Willie Cook, Ray Nance, Clark Terry (tp), Quentin Jackson, John Sanders, Britt Woodman (tb), Johnny Hodges, Russell Procope, Jimmy Hamilton, Paul Gonsalves, Harry Carney (sax), Jimmy Woode (b), Sam Woodyard (ds)

swing.note: A document of the first jazz concert ever held in a hall reserved for classical music. The night the "King of Swing" established jazz as concert-stage music.
swing.personnel: Benny Goodman (cl), Harry James, Ziggy Elman, Chris Griffin (tp), Red Ballard, Vernon Brown (tb), Hymie Schertzer, George Koenig (as), Art Rollini, Babe Russin (ts), Jess Stacy (p), Allan Reuss (g), Harry Goodman (b), Gene Krupa (ds). Count Basie (p) and Lester Young (ts) sat in for the jam session.

swing.note: Recordings that include one of the swing era's biggest hits, from a master clarinetist. Emblematic of the big-band era at the height of its popularity.
swing.personnel: Artie Shaw (cl), Chuck Peterson, John Best (tp), George Arus, Harry Rodgers (tb), Les Robinson, Hank Freeman (as), Tony Pastor, Ronnie Perry (ts), Les Burness (p), Al Avola (g), Sid Weiss (b), Cliff Leeman (ds)

swing.note: A large-scale suite that set out to portray African American history in music. Ellington pushed the big band beyond dance music toward art music.
swing.personnel: Duke Ellington (p), Wallace Jones, Rex Stewart, Ray Nance (tp), Lawrence Brown, Joe Nanton, Juan Tizol (tb), Johnny Hodges, Otto Hardwick, Barney Bigard, Ben Webster, Harry Carney (sax), Fred Guy (g), Junior Raglin (b), Sonny Greer (ds)

swing.note: Recordings by a band celebrated for its buoyant, polished arrangements and visually striking stagecraft. An ideal expression of swing as dance music.
swing.personnel: Jimmie Lunceford (leader), Sy Oliver (arr, tp), Eddie Tompkins, Paul Webster (tp), Trummy Young, Elmer Crumbley (tb), Willie Smith (as), Joe Thomas (ts), Edwin Wilcox (p), Al Norris (g), Moses Allen (b), Jimmy Crawford (ds)

swing.note: Sharp, driving recordings by the drummer-bandleader who held court at the Savoy Ballroom. This was also the band that discovered a young Ella Fitzgerald.
swing.personnel: Chick Webb (ds), Mario Bauza, Taft Jordan (tp), Sandy Williams (tb), Hilton Jefferson, Pete Clark (as), Wayman Carver (ts, fl), Tommy Fulford (p), Bobby Johnson (g), Beverly Peer (b), Ella Fitzgerald (vo)

swing.note: The bandleader's signature song, driven by theatrical scat-singing showmanship that swept the nation. Shows swing's highly entertainment-oriented side.
swing.personnel: Cab Calloway (vo, leader), Lammar Wright (tp), DePriest Wheeler (tb), Andrew Brown (cl), Walter Thomas (sax), Earres Prince (p), Morris White (banjo), Jimmy Smith (tuba), Leroy Maxey (ds)

swing.note: An uptempo jump number from the vibraphonist. Packed with the exuberance that would soon feed into rhythm and blues.
swing.personnel: Lionel Hampton (vib), Ernie Royal, Joe Newman (tp), Fred Beckett (tb), Marshall Royal (as), Illinois Jacquet (ts), Milt Buckner (p), Billy Mackel (g), Vernon Alley (b), George Jenkins (ds)

swing.note: A recording that paired the trombonist's smooth ensemble sound with a young Frank Sinatra's vocals, showcasing refined ballad expression.
swing.personnel: Tommy Dorsey (tb), Frank Sinatra (vo), The Pied Pipers (vo), Joe Bushkin (p), Clark Yocum (g), Sid Weiss (b), Buddy Rich (ds)

swing.note: A breathless record by the fiery band nicknamed "the Herd." Herman's outfit kept swing's energy burning right up to the eve of bebop.
swing.personnel: Woody Herman (cl, as, vo), Pete Candoli, Sonny Berman (tp), Bill Harris (tb), Flip Phillips (ts), Ralph Burns (p), Billy Bauer (g), Chubby Jackson (b), Dave Tough (ds)

swing.note: A popular number from the bandleader who wielded a brilliant trumpet tone as his signature weapon. Combines classical technique with broad popular appeal.
swing.personnel: Harry James (tp, leader) and his newly formed orchestra (records of individual sidemen are sparse, but the lineup included the era's featured vocalists)

swing.note: Recordings by a Kansas City-based band whose sound was shaped by Mary Lou Williams's sophisticated arrangements.
swing.personnel: Andy Kirk (leader, bass sax), Mary Lou Williams (p, arr), Harry Lawson, Earl Thompson (tp), Ted Donnelly (tb), John Harrington (cl, as), Dick Wilson (ts), Ted Brinson (b), Ben Thigpen (ds)

swing.note: The signature tune later famously covered by the Glenn Miller band, recorded here by its originator. A strongly blues-inflected take on swing.
swing.personnel: Erskine Hawkins (tp), Dud Bascomb (tp), Bill Johnson (as), Paul Bascomb (ts), Avery Parrish (p), William McLemore (b), James Morrison (ds)

swing.note: A band recording steeped in Kansas City's blues-heavy swing, notable also for featuring a young Charlie Parker in its ranks.
swing.personnel: Jay McShann (p), Charlie Parker (as), Orville Minor, Bernard Anderson (tp), Joe Taswell Baird (tb), John Jackson (as), Bob Mabane (ts), Gene Ramey (b), Gus Johnson (ds), Walter Brown (vo)

swing.note: A record by the pioneering leader who built the foundational grammar of big-band arranging, later inherited by Benny Goodman's orchestra.
swing.personnel: Fletcher Henderson (p, arr), Red Allen, Russell Smith, Irving Randolph (tp), Claude Jones, Keg Johnson (tb), Buster Bailey (cl), Hilton Jefferson (as), Coleman Hawkins (ts), John Kirby (b), Walter Johnson (ds)

vocal-jazz.album: Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Song Book
vocal-jazz.note: A landmark entry in the Song Book series. Fitzgerald's superb scatting and vocal technique helped define the "Great American Songbook."
vocal-jazz.personnel: Ella Fitzgerald (vo), Buddy Bregman (arr, cond) and orchestra

vocal-jazz.note: A devastating late-career album in which Holiday turns her worn, fragile voice into pure expressiveness. The pinnacle of vocal jazz conveyed through phrasing and space alone.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Billie Holiday (vo), Ray Ellis & His Orchestra (arr, cond), Mal Waldron (p, uncredited)

vocal-jazz.note: A landmark pairing of Vaughan's towering range and bebop-derived phrasing with a young Clifford Brown.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Sarah Vaughan (vo), Clifford Brown (tp), Herbie Mann (fl), Paul Quinichette (ts), Jimmy Jones (p), Joe Benjamin (b), Roy Haynes (ds)

vocal-jazz.note: An intimate small-combo album from a singer who was also an accomplished pianist. Cole served as a bridge between pop and jazz.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Nat King Cole (p, vo), Sweets Edison (tp), Willie Smith (as), John Collins (g), Charlie Harris (b), Lee Young (ds)

vocal-jazz.note: A pioneering concept album exploring heartbreak with unified thematic coherence. Sinatra elevated jazz phrasing into popular vocal art.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Frank Sinatra (vo), Nelson Riddle (arr, cond) and orchestra

vocal-jazz.note: A collection of Broadway numbers from the singer known as "The Velvet Fog" for his soft-grained voice. Its sophisticated interplay with the big band is the highlight.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Mel Tormé (vo), Marty Paich (arr, cond) and his "Dek-tette"

vocal-jazz.note: A live album showcasing the singer's cool, dry tone and sharp rhythmic instincts. Her intelligent, unsentimental scatting gives the record its distinctive personality.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Anita O'Day (vo) with a trio including John Poole (ds)

vocal-jazz.album: Sings Lover Man and Other Billie Holiday Classics
vocal-jazz.note: McRae brings her own interpretive stamp to the repertoire of the singer she revered, Billie Holiday, resulting in a record that is anything but mere imitation.
A live recording by the singer who pioneered a boldly improvisational vocal style, freely reshaping tempo and melody. Carter elevated vocal jazz to the level of instrumental improvisation.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Betty Carter (vo), John Hicks (p), Curtis Lundy (b), Kenny Washington (ds)

vocal-jazz.note: The defining work of the group that pioneered "vocalese" — setting lyrics to instrumental big-band recordings. Their three-part unison singing is a staggering technical feat.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Dave Lambert, Jon Hendricks, Annie Ross (vo). Backed by the Count Basie rhythm section (Nat Pierce (p), Freddie Green (g), Eddie Jones (b), Sonny Payne (ds)), recorded separately.

vocal-jazz.note: An all-star live album from the singer known as "Queen of the Blues," whose expressive range spanned both R&B and jazz.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Dinah Washington (vo), Clifford Brown (tp), Clark Terry (tp), Harold Land (ts), Junior Mance (p), Keter Betts (b), Max Roach (ds)

vocal-jazz.album: Count Basie Swings, Joe Williams Sings
vocal-jazz.note: A defining record from the Basie band's featured vocalist, whose blues-shouting power and swing feel meld seamlessly with the orchestra.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Joe Williams (vo), Count Basie (p) and orchestra

vocal-jazz.note: The debut from a singer who carried the vocalese tradition of setting poetic, improvised lyrics into the present day, introducing a new generation of male vocalist combining intellect and passion.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Kurt Elling (vo), Laurence Hobgood (p), Rob Amster (b), Michael Raynor (ds)

vocal-jazz.note: Reinterprets vintage standards through sophisticated orchestral arrangements built around Krall's piano-and-vocal core. A commercially successful example of modern jazz vocals.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Diana Krall (vo, p), Christian McBride (b), Peter Erskine / Jeff Hamilton (ds), Anthony Wilson (g), Claus Ogerman (arr, orchestra)

vocal-jazz.note: An experimental album blending acoustic textures with blues and folk idioms, opening new territory for jazz vocals.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Cassandra Wilson (vo), Brandon Ross (g), Chris Whitley (g), Kevin Breit (g), Lonnie Plaxico (b), Cyro Baptista (perc)

vocal-jazz.note: A defining work by a singer known for his singular scat style, using his voice like a percussion instrument. Jarreau glided effortlessly across the line between pop and jazz vocals.
vocal-jazz.personnel: Al Jarreau (vo), Jay Graydon (g, prod), Larry Williams (kbds), Abraham Laboriel (b), Steve Gadd (ds)

bebop.note: The legendary live meeting of Parker, Gillespie, Bud Powell, Charles Mingus, and Max Roach. A single night that captured bebop in its fully realized form.
bebop.personnel: Charlie Parker (as), Dizzy Gillespie (tp), Bud Powell (p), Charles Mingus (b), Max Roach (ds)

bebop.note: A definitive early-bebop recording from Gillespie's co-led combo with Charlie Parker. Its dizzying tempos and complex harmonies upended existing notions of jazz.
bebop.personnel: Dizzy Gillespie (tp), Charlie Parker (as), Clyde Hart (p), Remo Palmieri (g), Slam Stewart (b), Cozy Cole (ds)

bebop.note: The record that established bebop piano vocabulary — fast single-note lines in the right hand against jagged, punctuated chords in the left.
bebop.personnel: Bud Powell (p), Curly Russell (b), Max Roach (ds). Fats Navarro (tp) and Sonny Rollins (ts) also appear on some tracks.

bebop.note: An early Blue Note collection showcasing a compositional and pianistic style unafraid of dissonance and daring silences. Distinctive even within bebop's own vocabulary.
bebop.personnel: Thelonious Monk (p), Idrees Sulieman / George Taitt (tp), Danny Quebec West / Sahib Shihab (as), Billy Smith (ts), Gene Ramey (b), Art Blakey (ds)

bebop.note: A reunion recording of Parker and Gillespie, showing that neither man's improvisational speed or structural command had faded past their prime.
bebop.personnel: Charlie Parker (as), Dizzy Gillespie (tp), Thelonious Monk (p), Curly Russell (b), Buddy Rich (ds)

bebop.note: Recordings from a trumpeter who died young, whose brilliant tone and flawless technique later influenced Clifford Brown.
bebop.personnel: Fats Navarro (tp), Ernie Henry (as), Charlie Rouse (ts), Tadd Dameron (p), Nelson Boyd (b), Shadow Wilson (ds)

bebop.note: A leader date from the drummer who established "modern drumming" by keeping time on the cymbal rather than the bass drum. Embodies bebop's rhythmic revolution.
bebop.personnel: Kenny Clarke (ds), Donald Byrd (tp), Charlie Rouse (ts), Ray Bryant (p), Wendell Marshall (b)

bebop.note: Early recordings by a saxophonist deeply influenced by Parker who nonetheless honed his own tenor and alto approach. A prime example of bebop's spreading vocabulary.
bebop.personnel: Sonny Stitt (as, ts), Bud Powell (p), J.J. Johnson (tb), Curly Russell (b), Max Roach (ds)

bebop.album: The Eminent Jay Jay Johnson, Vol. 1
bebop.note: A leader date from the pioneer who made bebop's high-speed phrases possible on trombone, upending the instrument's reputation as unwieldy.
bebop.personnel: J.J. Johnson (tb), Clifford Brown (tp), Jimmy Heath (ts), John Lewis (p), Percy Heath (b), Kenny Clarke (ds)

bebop.note: An ambitious suite from a composer-minded pianist, bringing sophisticated harmony and orchestration into bebop's vocabulary.
bebop.personnel: Tadd Dameron (p, comp), Kenny Dorham (tp), Sahib Shihab (as, fl), Henry Coker (tb), Joe Alexander (ts), Cecil Payne (bs), John Simmons (b), Shadow Wilson (ds)

bebop.note: A trio date from a pianist also known as a sensitive accompanist on Parker's and Gillespie's sessions, marked by elegant, lyrical touch.
bebop.personnel: Al Haig (p), Bill Crow (b), Lee Abrams (ds)

bebop.note: An early leader date from the player who brought bebop phrasing to the vibraphone, coaxing warmth out of an instrument prone to a hard, metallic sound.
bebop.personnel: Milt Jackson (vib), John Lewis (p), Percy Heath (b), Kenny Clarke (ds). Lou Donaldson (as) appears on some tracks.

bebop.note: Early recordings by the pioneer who fully introduced bebop vocabulary to the tenor saxophone, distinguished by a big, resonant tone and unhurried phrasing.
bebop.personnel: Dexter Gordon (ts), Leonard Hawkins (tp), Sadik Hakim / Bud Powell (p), Curly Russell (b), Max Roach (ds)

bebop.note: A leader date from the bassist who opened up the instrument's potential as a solo voice. His skill on cello also adds distinctive color to the ensemble.
bebop.personnel: Oscar Pettiford (b, cello), Julius Watkins (french horn), Gigi Gryce (as, fl), Walter Bishop Jr. (p), Percy Brice (ds)

bebop.note: A follow-up Blue Note session known for its undimmed drive and creativity, recorded even as Powell struggled with declining mental and physical health.
bebop.personnel: Bud Powell (p), George Duvivier (b), Art Taylor (ds)

bebop.note: A live recording reconstructing bebop for big-band format, capturing the vitality of Gillespie's "jazz ambassador" era, which included State Department-sponsored overseas tours.
bebop.personnel: Dizzy Gillespie (tp) and big band: Lee Morgan, Ernie Royal (tp), Melba Liston (tb), Ernie Henry (as), Billy Mitchell (ts), Wynton Kelly (p), Paul West (b), Charli Persip (ds)

latin-jazz.note: Groundbreaking recordings born from Gillespie's encounter with the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo, fusing bebop with Afro-Cuban rhythms.
latin-jazz.personnel: Dizzy Gillespie (tp), Chano Pozo (conga), James Moody (ts), Milt Jackson (vib), John Lewis (p), Al McKibbon (b), Kenny Clarke (ds)

latin-jazz.note: A defining big-band statement from "the King of Mambo," fusing Latin percussion with jazz horn arrangements into a single, seamless whole.
latin-jazz.personnel: Tito Puente (timbales), Santos Colon (vo), Jose Madera (sax, arr) and the Puente big band

latin-jazz.note: The landmark album that introduced bossa nova to American jazz audiences at large. The hit "The Girl from Ipanema" fueled a full-blown Latin jazz boom.
latin-jazz.personnel: Stan Getz (ts), João Gilberto (g, vo), Astrud Gilberto (vo), Antonio Carlos Jobim (p), Tommy Williams (b), Milton Banana (ds)

latin-jazz.note: A vibraphonist's crossroads of Latin jazz and soul jazz, balancing pop accessibility with Latin groove.
latin-jazz.personnel: Cal Tjader (vib), Clare Fischer (p), Willie Bobo (timbales), Armando Peraza (conga), Al McKibbon (b), Johnny Rae (ds)

latin-jazz.note: A defining work from the big band that laid the foundations of Afro-Cuban jazz, its dense brass and percussion combining into a fiercely energetic whole.
latin-jazz.personnel: Machito (vo, maracas), Mario Bauza (tp, arr), Doc Cheatham (tp), Jose Mangual (bongo), Ubaldo Nieto (timbales), Candido Camero (conga), Rene Hernandez (p)

latin-jazz.note: The percussionist turned Herbie Hancock's tune into a Latin-grooved hit, an emblem of the fusion between soul jazz and Latin jazz.
latin-jazz.personnel: Mongo Santamaria (conga), Marty Sheller (tp), Bobby Capers (as, fl), Rodgers Grant (p), Victor Venegas (b), Frankie Malabe (ds)

latin-jazz.note: An ambitious work from the composer-arranger who fused classical technique with Afro-Cuban rhythms in suite form, expanding Latin jazz's artistic ambitions.
latin-jazz.personnel: Chico O'Farrill (arr, comp), leading the Machito orchestra with guest appearances by Charlie Parker (as), Flip Phillips (ts), and Buddy Rich (ds)

latin-jazz.note: An instrumental album by bossa nova's chief architect himself, its restrained, composerly aesthetic reflected throughout the orchestration.
latin-jazz.personnel: Antonio Carlos Jobim (p, g) fronting a small ensemble and orchestra

latin-jazz.note: The tenor sax-and-guitar album that introduced bossa nova stateside. The hit "Desafinado" sparked America's bossa nova craze.
latin-jazz.personnel: Stan Getz (ts), Charlie Byrd (g), Keter Betts (b), Buddy Deppenschmidt (ds), Gene Byrd (g)

latin-jazz.note: An ambitious work from the pianist-bandleader who boldly fused salsa with jazz vocabulary, expanding the possibilities of improvisation within Latin music.
latin-jazz.personnel: Eddie Palmieri (p), Lalo Rodriguez (vo), Ismael Quintana (vo), Alfredo "Chocolate" Armenteros (tp), Andy Gonzalez (b), Nicky Marrero (timbales)

latin-jazz.album: Cal Tjader Plays the Contemporary Music of Mexico and Brazil
latin-jazz.note: A vibraphonist's wide-ranging survey of Latin American music, absorbing diverse rhythms into a jazz vocabulary.
latin-jazz.personnel: Cal Tjader (vib) leading a Latin jazz sextet

latin-jazz.note: A live recording at the jazz shrine from the bandleader who helped drive the mambo craze, combining dance-music functionality with performance depth.
latin-jazz.personnel: Tito Rodríguez (vo, leader) and mambo orchestra

latin-jazz.note: A congero's crossroads of Latin jazz and boogaloo, driven by percussion-forward groove.
latin-jazz.personnel: Ray Barretto (conga) leading a boogaloo/charanga-style band

latin-jazz.note: A fine example of Latin soul jazz from the timbalero, its urbane, polished groove also winning favor on the club scene.
latin-jazz.personnel: Willie Bobo (timbales, vo), Melvin Lastie (cornet), Victor Pantoja (conga), Bobby Montez (vib, marimba), and rhythm section

latin-jazz.note: An ambitious work from the percussionist who brought Afro-Cuban ritual rhythms into jazz's orbit, marked by an almost incantatory intensity.
latin-jazz.personnel: Sabu Martinez (conga, vo) with an ensemble of Cuban folkloric musicians, including Arsenio Rodriguez (tres) on some tracks

latin-jazz.note: One of the defining works from the congero who inherited Cal Tjader's Latin jazz legacy, carrying traditional Afro-Cuban jazz forward into the modern era.
latin-jazz.personnel: Poncho Sanchez (conga), Ramon Banda (ds), Tony Banda (b), David Torres (p), Steve Huffsteter (tp)

cool-jazz.note: A compilation of the 1949-50 nonet sessions. Its restrained tone and arrangement, in contrast to bebop's intensity, launched an entirely new current in jazz.
cool-jazz.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), Gerry Mulligan (bs), Lee Konitz (as), J.J. Johnson / Kai Winding (tb), Junior Collins / Gunther Schuller (french horn), Bill Barber (tuba), John Lewis / Al Haig (p), Nelson Boyd / Joe Shulman (b), Max Roach / Kenny Clarke (ds)

cool-jazz.note: A daring experiment in odd time signatures that, thanks to the massive hit "Take Five," became one of the best-selling jazz albums of all time.
cool-jazz.personnel: Dave Brubeck (p), Paul Desmond (as), Eugene Wright (b), Joe Morello (ds)

cool-jazz.note: An unusual album in which the trumpeter's own whispery vocals caused a stir. Embodies the delicate aesthetic of West Coast jazz.
cool-jazz.personnel: Chet Baker (tp, vo), Russ Freeman (p), Carson Smith (b), Bob Neel (ds)

cool-jazz.album: The Original Quartet with Chet Baker
cool-jazz.note: Working without a piano, this quartet created a cool, airy sound built on the contrapuntal interplay of baritone sax and trumpet.
cool-jazz.personnel: Gerry Mulligan (bs), Chet Baker (tp), Carson Smith / Bob Whitlock (b), Chico Hamilton (ds)

cool-jazz.note: An experimental album from the cerebral pianist who boldly employed overdubbing and tape editing. Represents cool jazz's intellectual side.
cool-jazz.personnel: Lennie Tristano (p, overdubs), Lee Konitz (as), Peter Ind (b), Jeff Morton (ds)

cool-jazz.note: Early recordings from a saxophonist who sought an alto vocabulary distinct from Parker's. His dry tone and linear phrasing embody the cool aesthetic.
cool-jazz.personnel: Lee Konitz (as), Lennie Tristano (p), Billy Bauer (g), Arnold Fishkin (b), Shelly Manne / Denzil Best (ds)

cool-jazz.note: An album that fully exploits the warm tenor tone that earned Getz the nickname "The Sound." Shows his natural affinity with polished West Coast session players.
cool-jazz.personnel: Stan Getz (ts), Bob Brookmeyer (tb), Conte Candoli (tp), Lou Levy (p), Leroy Vinnegar (b), Shelly Manne (ds)

cool-jazz.note: An elegant record from the Brubeck band's alto man, including an odd-meter sequel to "Take Five." Light, poetic tone is the hallmark.
cool-jazz.personnel: Paul Desmond (as), Jim Hall (g), Gene Cherico (b), Connie Kay (ds)

cool-jazz.note: A big-band album from the composer-arranger-trumpeter who was a pillar of West Coast cool jazz, balancing intricate voicings with a relaxed feel.
cool-jazz.personnel: Shorty Rogers (tp, arr) and His Giants (a big band of West Coast musicians)

cool-jazz.note: A pioneering example of reimagining musical-theater songs through a jazz trio. That the leader is a drummer also reflects West Coast jazz's flexibility.
cool-jazz.personnel: Shelly Manne (ds), André Previn (p), Leroy Vinnegar (b)

cool-jazz.note: A drummerless album pursuing chamber-music-like stillness, from a clarinet/saxophone player with a distinctive folkloric melodic sensibility.
cool-jazz.personnel: Jimmy Giuffre (cl, ts, bs), Jim Hall (g), Ralph Peña (b)

cool-jazz.note: A chamber-jazz ensemble that fused classical counterpoint with the blues. Its elegy for Django Reinhardt became its signature piece.
cool-jazz.personnel: John Lewis (p), Milt Jackson (vib), Percy Heath (b), Connie Kay (ds)

cool-jazz.note: A West Coast cool jazz classic recorded in a single session with Miles Davis's rhythm section. Tension and improvisational spark coexist throughout.
cool-jazz.personnel: Art Pepper (as), Red Garland (p), Paul Chambers (b), Philly Joe Jones (ds)

cool-jazz.note: A work from the drummer-leader who pursued a chamber-music texture with an unusual lineup including cello and flute. Shows the diversity within West Coast jazz.
cool-jazz.personnel: Chico Hamilton (ds), Buddy Collette (reeds, fl), Jim Hall (g), Fred Katz (cello), Carson Smith (b)

cool-jazz.note: An urbane, shadow-laced vocal album from a singer who came up through the Kenton band. Embodies cool jazz's aesthetic through the voice.
An album from a tenor player who sang swing vocabulary with a cool touch, marked by unpretentious, naturally flowing phrasing.
cool-jazz.personnel: Zoot Sims (ts), Dave McKenna (p), Wyatt Ruther (b), Gus Johnson (ds)

hard-bop.note: The definitive hard bop statement, restoring gospel and blues grit to bebop. A signature work from a band that remained a proving ground for young talent for decades.
hard-bop.personnel: Art Blakey (ds), Lee Morgan (tp), Benny Golson (ts), Bobby Timmons (p), Jymie Merritt (b)

hard-bop.note: The title track, written as a tribute to Silver's father, fuses a Latin rhythm with a funky groove. Distills hard bop's warm accessibility into a single track.
hard-bop.personnel: Horace Silver (p), Carmell Jones (tp), Joe Henderson (ts), Teddy Smith (b), Roger Humphries (ds)

hard-bop.note: A landmark leader date showcasing the calypso-tinged melody of "St. Thomas" alongside Rollins's ability to build a solo through continuous thematic development.
hard-bop.personnel: Sonny Rollins (ts), Tommy Flanagan (p), Doug Watkins (b), Max Roach (ds)

hard-bop.note: A co-led date from the trumpeter who died tragically young and the drummer, pairing a brilliant tone with flawless technique. A key early hard-bop statement.
hard-bop.personnel: Clifford Brown (tp), Max Roach (ds), Harold Land (ts), Richie Powell (p), George Morrow (b)

hard-bop.note: An unusual date featuring Miles Davis as a sideman. Known for its classic reading of "Autumn Leaves," balancing sophistication with accessibility.
hard-bop.personnel: Cannonball Adderley (as), Miles Davis (tp), Hank Jones (p), Sam Jones (b), Art Blakey (ds)

hard-bop.note: An early leader date from the young trumpeter, notable for its lyrical ballad playing. Shows the growth that would lead to "The Sidewinder."
hard-bop.personnel: Lee Morgan (tp), Sonny Clark (p), Doug Watkins (b), Art Taylor (ds)

hard-bop.note: A substantial record from the young trumpeter who combined a brilliant tone with overwhelming technique, symbolizing hard bop's high performance standards.
hard-bop.personnel: Freddie Hubbard (tp), Bernard McKinney (euphonium), Wayne Shorter (ts), McCoy Tyner (p), Art Davis (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

hard-bop.note: A defining work from a tenor saxophonist praised as a musician's musician. Mature melodic sense and relaxed swing feel are the appeal.
hard-bop.personnel: Hank Mobley (ts), Wynton Kelly (p), Paul Chambers (b), Art Blakey (ds)

hard-bop.note: A pivotal work from an altoist steeped in Parker's lineage who also reached toward free jazz. Pushed the boundaries of hard bop.
hard-bop.personnel: Jackie McLean (as), Walter Davis Jr. (p), Herbie Lewis (b), Billy Higgins (ds)

hard-bop.note: A leader date from a player known for solid compositional craft and richly expressive trumpet playing. A fine example of hard bop that impresses through structure rather than flash.
hard-bop.personnel: Kenny Dorham (tp), Hank Mobley (ts), Kenny Drew (p), Paul Chambers (b), Philly Joe Jones (ds)

hard-bop.note: Shorter's first Blue Note leader date. Mysterious compositions intersect with hard-bop vocabulary, foreshadowing his later style.
hard-bop.personnel: Wayne Shorter (ts), Lee Morgan (tp), McCoy Tyner (p), Reggie Workman (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

hard-bop.note: Henderson's debut, including "Blue Bossa." Skillfully blends Latin rhythmic feel with hard bop's tension.
hard-bop.personnel: Joe Henderson (ts), Kenny Dorham (tp), McCoy Tyner (p), Butch Warren (b), Pete La Roca (ds)

hard-bop.note: A leader date from the pianist who made his name as the composer behind "funky jazz" in the Jazz Messengers. Gospel-derived buoyancy is the calling card.
hard-bop.personnel: Bobby Timmons (p), Sam Jones (b), Jimmy Cobb (ds)

hard-bop.note: The debut of the trumpet-and-tenor co-led band, marked by careful arrangements and a well-balanced ensemble sound.
hard-bop.personnel: Art Farmer (tp), Benny Golson (ts), Curtis Fuller (tb), McCoy Tyner (p), Addison Farmer (b), Lex Humphries (ds)

hard-bop.note: A record from the trumpeter combining solid stylistic craft with youthful drive. Shows straight-ahead hard bop before his later turn to funk.
hard-bop.personnel: Donald Byrd (tp), Jackie McLean (as), Charlie Rouse (ts), Pepper Adams (bs), Walter Davis Jr. (p), Sam Jones (b), Art Taylor (ds)

hard-bop.note: A leader date from a trumpeter known for a warm tone and songful phrasing. Values feeling over flash.
hard-bop.personnel: Blue Mitchell (tp), Wynton Kelly (p), Sam Jones (b), Roy Brooks (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A signature work from the player who established the Hammond organ as a lead voice in jazz. Develops gospel-rooted groove through extended collective improvisation.
soul-jazz.personnel: Jimmy Smith (org), Lee Morgan (tp), Lou Donaldson (as), Kenny Burrell (g), Art Blakey (ds), Tina Brooks (ts, on an alternate take)

soul-jazz.note: The boogaloo-flavored title track became an unexpected hit, helping bolster Blue Note's commercial fortunes.
soul-jazz.personnel: Lee Morgan (tp), Joe Henderson (ts), Barry Harris (p), Bob Cranshaw (b), Billy Higgins (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A live recording from the Montreux Jazz Festival. The groove of "Compared to What" marked a meeting point between soul jazz and funk.
soul-jazz.personnel: Les McCann (p, vo), Eddie Harris (ts), Benny Bailey (tp), Leroy Vinnegar (b), Donald Dean (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A live cover version that reached the national pop charts — a rare achievement, and a prime example of soul jazz's crossover appeal.
soul-jazz.personnel: Ramsey Lewis (p), Eldee Young (b), Redd Holt (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A leader date from a tenor player steeped in blues and gospel vocabulary. His thick, rich tone embodies soul jazz's warmth.
soul-jazz.personnel: Stanley Turrentine (ts), Les McCann (p), Bob Cranshaw (b), Otis Finch (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A signature work from a guitarist known for building solos out of simple, exact phrases. The title track's extended, unhurried development leaves a meditative afterglow.
soul-jazz.personnel: Grant Green (g), Bobby Hutcherson (vib), Joe Henderson (ts), Duke Pearson (p), Bob Cranshaw (b), Al Harewood (ds)

soul-jazz.note: An album from the guitarist who forged a singular vocabulary using thumb-picking and octaves, expressing soul jazz's warmth in an organ-trio setting.
soul-jazz.personnel: Wes Montgomery (g), Mel Rhyne (org), Jimmy Cobb (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A leader date from the organist who pushed the Hammond's thick groove to the fore, also known for the venue it gave to young talents like George Benson.
soul-jazz.personnel: Jack McDuff (org), Grant Green (g), Red Holloway (ts), Ben Dixon (ds)

soul-jazz.note: An album linking funk's heavier rhythms to organ-driven groove, marking soul jazz's transition into the 1970s.
soul-jazz.personnel: Charles Earland (org), Virgil Jones (tp), Houston Person (ts), Melvin Sparks (g), Idris Muhammad (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A defining record from the organist who fused boogaloo with organ jazz. Its danceable groove has been rediscovered by club audiences.
soul-jazz.personnel: Reuben Wilson (org), Grant Green (g), Lee Morgan (tp), George Coleman (ts), Idris Muhammad (ds)

soul-jazz.note: An album from a player whose thick, welcoming tenor tone makes standards sing. Embodies soul jazz's aesthetic of feeling over technique.
soul-jazz.personnel: Houston Person (ts), Sonny Phillips (org), Billy Butler (g), Frank Jones (b), Frankie Jones (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A defining work from the woman organist known as "Queen of the Organ," marked by well-balanced swing and elegant groove.
soul-jazz.personnel: Shirley Scott (org), Stanley Turrentine (ts), George Tucker (b), Roy Brooks (ds)

soul-jazz.note: An accessible, groove-focused album from a Hammond organ master. Its jukebox-friendly ease reflects one facet of soul jazz.
soul-jazz.personnel: Johnny Hammond Smith (org), Houston Person (ts), Thornel Schwartz (g), Joe Dukes (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A signature work from a player who won popularity with a bold, blues-drenched tenor tone, making simple melodies sing with conviction.
soul-jazz.personnel: Gene Ammons (ts), Tommy Flanagan (p), Doug Watkins (b), Art Taylor (ds), Ray Barretto (conga)

soul-jazz.album: Mercy, Mercy, Mercy! Live at "The Club"
soul-jazz.note: A live album whose Joe Zawinul-penned title track became a huge hit. Its gospel-and-funk exuberance embodies soul jazz's festive spirit.
soul-jazz.personnel: Cannonball Adderley (as), Nat Adderley (cornet), Joe Zawinul (p, elp), Victor Gaskin (b), Roy McCurdy (ds)

soul-jazz.note: A defining work from an organist known for a powerful, low-slung groove. True to its title, this record embodies soul jazz's essence.
soul-jazz.personnel: Richard "Groove" Holmes (org), Les McCann (p, on some tracks), Gene Edwards (g), George Randall (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A revolutionary work built on modal scales rather than chord changes as the basis for improvisation. One of the best-selling jazz albums ever and the wellspring of modal jazz.
modal-jazz.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), John Coltrane (ts), Cannonball Adderley (as), Bill Evans (p; Wynton Kelly on "Freddie Freeloader"), Paul Chambers (b), Jimmy Cobb (ds)

modal-jazz.note: Transforms a musical-theater tune into an extended modal improvisation on soprano saxophone. A turning point in Coltrane's ongoing exploration.
modal-jazz.personnel: John Coltrane (ss, ts), McCoy Tyner (p), Steve Davis (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A suite expressing gratitude for religious faith. This towering achievement in jazz history joins modal playing with spiritual searching.
modal-jazz.personnel: John Coltrane (ts), McCoy Tyner (p), Jimmy Garrison (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A leader date from the Coltrane Quartet's pianist, refining quartal harmony and modal playing into his own distinctive vocabulary.
modal-jazz.personnel: McCoy Tyner (p), Joe Henderson (ts), Ron Carter (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

modal-jazz.note: An ambitious work that expands modal playing into a grander sound with a large brass ensemble.
modal-jazz.personnel: John Coltrane (ts, ss), McCoy Tyner (p), Reggie Workman / Art Davis (b), Elvin Jones (ds), large brass ensemble arranged by Eric Dolphy

modal-jazz.note: A pivotal work whose title track anticipates a modal approach, laying the groundwork for "Kind of Blue."
modal-jazz.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), John Coltrane (ts), Cannonball Adderley (as), Red Garland (p), Paul Chambers (b), Philly Joe Jones (ds)

modal-jazz.note: An early leader date from the pianist known for delicate harmonic sense and masterful use of space, recorded just before he joined Miles Davis's band.
modal-jazz.personnel: Bill Evans (p), Sam Jones (b), Philly Joe Jones (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A leader date balancing modal song structures with accessible melody, showcasing Shorter's maturity as a composer.
modal-jazz.personnel: Wayne Shorter (ts), Herbie Hancock (p), Reggie Workman (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A leader date from the drummer known for the multi-layered polyrhythms that anchored the Coltrane Quartet, showing modal jazz's rhythmic freedom.
modal-jazz.personnel: Elvin Jones (ds), Thad Jones (tp), Frank Foster (ts), Hank Jones (p), Art Davis (b)

modal-jazz.note: A spiritually charged, exultant suite that includes "The Creator Has a Master Plan." Embodies the meeting of modal jazz and free jazz.
modal-jazz.personnel: Pharoah Sanders (ts), Leon Thomas (vo), Julius Watkins (french horn), James Spaulding (fl), Lonnie Liston Smith (p), Reggie Workman / Ron Carter (b), Billy Hart (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A meditative sound world built around harp and Eastern modal scales. Further expands modal jazz's spiritual dimension.
modal-jazz.personnel: Alice Coltrane (harp, p), Pharoah Sanders (ss), Cecil McBee (b), Rashied Ali (ds), Tulsi (tambura)

modal-jazz.note: A pioneering work incorporating Middle Eastern and Asian instruments and scales into jazz. An early embodiment of modal jazz's openness to other cultures.
modal-jazz.personnel: Yusef Lateef (ts, fl, oboe), Barry Harris (p), Ernie Farrow (b, rabat), Lex Humphries (ds)

modal-jazz.album: At the Pershing: But Not for Me
modal-jazz.note: A live album from a pianist known for a spare style built on bold use of space and silence, said to have influenced Miles Davis.
modal-jazz.personnel: Ahmad Jamal (p), Israel Crosby (b), Vernel Fournier (ds)

modal-jazz.note: An ambitious work from the trumpeter combining modal vocabulary with somewhat experimental composition, showing his growth beyond hard bop.
modal-jazz.personnel: Freddie Hubbard (tp), James Spaulding (as, fl), Ronnie Mathews (p), Eddie Khan (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A large-ensemble work featuring brass from the pianist known for quartal harmony, expanding modal jazz's sound into orchestral territory.
modal-jazz.personnel: McCoy Tyner (p), Lee Morgan (tp), Julian Priester (tb), James Spaulding (as, fl), Bennie Maupin (ts, bcl), Herbie Lewis (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

modal-jazz.note: A little-recorded but highly regarded leader date from a trombonist, marked by dark, hard-edged sound moving between modal jazz and free playing.
modal-jazz.personnel: Grachan Moncur III (tb), Lee Morgan (tp), Jackie McLean (as), Bobby Hutcherson (vib), Bob Cranshaw (b), Tony Williams (ds)

free-jazz.album: The Shape of Jazz to Come
free-jazz.note: A controversial, era-defining work that presented improvisation freed from set chord changes. As its title promised, it foretold the direction jazz would take.
free-jazz.personnel: Ornette Coleman (as), Don Cherry (cornet), Charlie Haden (b), Billy Higgins (ds)

free-jazz.note: A bold structure featuring two quartets improvising simultaneously. The very source of the genre name "free jazz."
free-jazz.personnel: Double quartet: Ornette Coleman (as), Don Cherry (cornet), Freddie Hubbard (tp), Eric Dolphy (bcl), Scott LaFaro / Charlie Haden (b), Billy Higgins / Ed Blackwell (ds)

free-jazz.note: A radical late-period Coltrane masterpiece built around extended, ferocious collective improvisation from a large ensemble.
free-jazz.personnel: John Coltrane (ts), Pharoah Sanders (ts), Archie Shepp (ts), Freddie Hubbard (tp), Dewey Johnson (tp), Marion Brown (as), John Tchicai (as), McCoy Tyner (p), Art Davis, Jimmy Garrison (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

free-jazz.note: Builds simple, folk- and march-like melodies into the foundation for screaming, ecstatic tenor saxophone improvisation. A work embodying free jazz's spiritual dimension.
free-jazz.personnel: Albert Ayler (ts), Gary Peacock (b), Sunny Murray (ds)

free-jazz.note: A defining work from a pianist known for his overwhelming technique and density in treating the piano as a percussion instrument. Structure and improvisation are held in fierce balance.
free-jazz.personnel: Cecil Taylor (p), Jimmy Lyons (as), Eddie Gale (tp), Ken McIntyre (as, bcl, oboe), Henry Grimes / Alan Silva (b), Andrew Cyrille (ds)

free-jazz.note: The final leader date from a multi-instrumentalist skilled on alto sax, bass clarinet, and flute. Angular rhythms and dissonance create a singular tension.
free-jazz.personnel: Eric Dolphy (as, bcl, fl), Freddie Hubbard (tp), Bobby Hutcherson (vib), Richard Davis (b), Tony Williams (ds)

free-jazz.album: The Heliocentric Worlds of Sun Ra, Vol. 1
free-jazz.note: A radical work from a big band incorporating electronic instruments and cosmic concepts, fusing free jazz with a science-fiction worldview.
free-jazz.personnel: Sun Ra (p, synth, and others), Marshall Allen (as), John Gilmore (ts), Pat Patrick (bs), Ronnie Boykins (b), Clifford Jarvis (ds)

free-jazz.note: A work from a tenor player deeply reflecting the political spirit of the civil rights era, uniting message and free improvisation.
free-jazz.personnel: Archie Shepp (ts), Ted Curson (tp), Marion Brown (as), Joseph Orange (tb), Reggie Workman (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

free-jazz.note: An ambitious work from the pocket-trumpet player, linking multiple pieces into a single unbroken suite. Brought new structural sensibility to free jazz.
free-jazz.personnel: Don Cherry (tp), Gato Barbieri (ts), Henry Grimes (b), Ed Blackwell (ds)

free-jazz.note: An ambitious work tackling the unprecedented format of a complete solo alto saxophone album, joining contemporary-classical vocabulary with free jazz improvisation.
An experimental work from a central figure of the AACM (Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians), prioritizing use of space over sheer density of sound.
free-jazz.personnel: Roscoe Mitchell (as), Lester Bowie (tp), Maurice McIntyre (ts), Lester Lashley (tb, cello), Malachi Favors (b)

free-jazz.note: An overtly political big-band work drawing on songs of resistance from the Spanish Civil War. A rare instance of free jazz joined with social message.
free-jazz.personnel: Charlie Haden (b), Carla Bley (p, arr), Don Cherry (tp), Gato Barbieri (ts), Dewey Redman (as), Roswell Rudd (tb)

free-jazz.note: A leader date from an altoist closely tied to Archie Shepp, carrying a lyrical, middle-ground appeal as it steps toward free improvisation without abandoning lyricism.
free-jazz.personnel: Marion Brown (as), Grachan Moncur III (tb), Dave Burrell (p), Norris Jones / Sirone (b), Beaver Harris (ds)

free-jazz.note: An album from a player who preserved traditional hard-bop form while dismantling it from within through his improvisation.
free-jazz.personnel: Sam Rivers (ts), Jaki Byard (p), Ron Carter (b), Tony Williams (ds)

free-jazz.note: An experimental work bringing together longtime associates and a new generation of players, expanding free jazz's vocabulary into greater diversity.
free-jazz.personnel: Ornette Coleman (as), Don Cherry / Bobby Bradford (cornet), Dewey Redman (ts), Charlie Haden (b), Ed Blackwell (ds)

free-jazz.note: Builds fierce improvisation on a foundation of simple military-march and hymn-like melodies, showcasing free jazz's own particular spirituality.
free-jazz.personnel: Albert Ayler (ts), Donald Ayler (tp), Charles Tyler (as), Call Cobbs (p, harpsichord), Gary Peacock (b), Sunny Murray (ds)

post-bop.note: A work that blends modal jazz and hard bop vocabulary into an increasingly personal compositional aesthetic. Distinctive mysterious song titles and structures.
post-bop.personnel: Wayne Shorter (ts), Freddie Hubbard (tp), Herbie Hancock (p), Ron Carter (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

post-bop.note: A concept album structured as a suite on an ocean theme. Refines modal playing into an open, lyrical sound.
post-bop.personnel: Herbie Hancock (p), Freddie Hubbard (tp), George Coleman (ts), Ron Carter (b), Tony Williams (ds)

post-bop.note: A hidden gem known for tense composing and arranging that walks a tightrope between traditional form and free improvisation.
post-bop.personnel: Andrew Hill (p), Kenny Dorham (tp), Eric Dolphy (as, fl, bcl), Joe Henderson (ts), Richard Davis (b), Tony Williams (ds)

post-bop.note: An experimental work built on the inverted idea of letting the rhythm section, rather than the soloists, take the lead. The pinnacle of the Second Great Quintet.
post-bop.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), Wayne Shorter (ts), Herbie Hancock (p), Ron Carter (b), Tony Williams (ds)

post-bop.note: A studio album of mostly original compositions from the Second Great Quintet. A turning point away from the standards-heavy repertoire of earlier years.
post-bop.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), Wayne Shorter (ts), Herbie Hancock (p), Ron Carter (b), Tony Williams (ds)

post-bop.note: A work from the quintet at its rhythmically freest, establishing the "time, no changes" approach that became central to their sound.
post-bop.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), Wayne Shorter (ts), Herbie Hancock (p), Ron Carter (b), Tony Williams (ds)

post-bop.note: A leader date including "Cantaloupe Island," where the fusion of modal playing and hard bop reaches polished fruition.
post-bop.personnel: Herbie Hancock (p), Freddie Hubbard (cornet), Ron Carter (b), Tony Williams (ds)

post-bop.note: A precocious leader date from a drumming prodigy who joined Miles Davis's band as a teenager, moving lightly between free playing and post-bop.
post-bop.personnel: Tony Williams (ds), Sam Rivers (ts), Herbie Hancock (p, on some tracks), Ron Carter / Gary Peacock (b), Bobby Hutcherson (vib)

post-bop.note: An avant-garde compositional statement from the vibraphonist, exploring sonic textures well beyond the instrument's conventional image.
post-bop.personnel: Bobby Hutcherson (vib), Freddie Hubbard (tp), Sam Rivers (reeds), Andrew Hill (p), Richard Davis (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

post-bop.note: An ambitious work from a trumpeter who freely commanded complex harmony and modal playing, representing the generation that further expanded post-bop vocabulary.
post-bop.personnel: Woody Shaw (tp), Bennie Maupin (ts, fl), George Cables (p), Ron Carter (b), Lenny White (ds)

post-bop.album: Now He Sings, Now He Sobs
post-bop.note: A defining work from before Corea's fusion period, showcasing outstanding improvisational power in an acoustic trio setting.
post-bop.personnel: Chick Corea (p), Miroslav Vitous (b), Roy Haynes (ds)

post-bop.note: A large-ensemble compositional work pursuing a mysterious, cosmic concept, reflecting Shorter's ambition as a composer beyond hard bop's boundaries.
post-bop.personnel: Wayne Shorter (ts), Freddie Hubbard (tp), James Spaulding (as), Grachan Moncur III (tb), Herbie Hancock (p), Ron Carter (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

post-bop.note: A defining work from the organist who brought modal playing and free vocabulary to the Hammond, sometimes described as "the organ equivalent of John Coltrane."
post-bop.personnel: Larry Young (org), Woody Shaw (tp), Joe Henderson (ts), Elvin Jones (ds)

post-bop.note: A work from the tenor player pushing modal song structures into tighter focus, marked by robust improvisation and rhythmic tension.
post-bop.personnel: Joe Henderson (ts), McCoy Tyner (p), Bob Cranshaw (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

post-bop.note: A work tightly weaving together traditional form and avant-garde improvisation, part of Blue Note's run of experimental recordings of the era.
post-bop.personnel: Sam Rivers (ts, fl), Freddie Hubbard (tp), Herbie Hancock (p), Ron Carter (b), Joe Chambers (ds)

post-bop.note: An ambitious work interpreting modal compositions on guitar, revealing a more introspective side than Green's usual soul-jazz output.
post-bop.personnel: Grant Green (g), McCoy Tyner (p), Bob Cranshaw (b), Elvin Jones (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: A boldly provocative work incorporating rock beats, electric instruments, and studio editing techniques, giving birth to the jazz fusion movement itself.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), Wayne Shorter (ss), Bennie Maupin (bcl), Chick Corea (elp), Joe Zawinul (elp), John McLaughlin (g), Dave Holland (b), Harvey Brooks (elb), Jack DeJohnette / Lenny White / Don Alias (ds), Airto Moreira (perc)

jazz-fusion.note: A record marking the fusion movement's peak, including the massive hit "Birdland." Intricate ensemble writing and improvisation coexist at the highest level.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Joe Zawinul (kbds), Wayne Shorter (sax), Jaco Pastorius (b), Alex Acuña (ds), Manolo Badrena (perc)

jazz-fusion.note: Boldly incorporated funk grooves and synthesizers, becoming one of the best-selling jazz albums of all time and proving fusion's commercial viability.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Herbie Hancock (kbds), Bennie Maupin (reeds), Paul Jackson (b), Harvey Mason (ds), Bill Summers (perc)

jazz-fusion.note: Fuses jazz and rock virtuosity through odd meters and blazing unison lines. A ferocious statement led by John McLaughlin's guitar.
jazz-fusion.personnel: John McLaughlin (g), Jan Hammer (kbds), Jerry Goodman (violin), Rick Laird (b), Billy Cobham (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: The debut of the group formed by Chick Corea, marked by light Brazilian-derived rhythms and electric textures.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Chick Corea (elp), Joe Farrell (sax, fl), Stanley Clarke (b), Airto Moreira (ds), Flora Purim (vo)

jazz-fusion.note: A sweeping concept album driven by synthesizers. Virtuosic exchanges and a fantasy-themed world represent one high point of fusion.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Chick Corea (kbds), Stanley Clarke (b), Al Di Meola (g), Lenny White (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: The debut of the group co-founded by Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter, blending free collective improvisation with electronics.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Joe Zawinul (kbds), Wayne Shorter (sax), Miroslav Vitous (b), Alphonse Mouzon (ds), Airto Moreira (perc)

jazz-fusion.note: A pioneering work built around organ and guitar, violently fusing rock and jazz into a fierce, driving groove.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Tony Williams (ds), John McLaughlin (g), Larry Young (org)

jazz-fusion.note: The first leader date, recorded in England, from the guitarist who would go on to lead the Mahavishnu Orchestra. Free jazz and rock vocabulary intersect.
jazz-fusion.personnel: John McLaughlin (g), John Surman (bs, ss), Brian Odgers (b), Tony Oxley (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: Introduces electric piano and guitar, pursuing a hushed, meditative texture. A transitional work heralding the fusion era.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Miles Davis (tp), Wayne Shorter (ss), Chick Corea (elp), Herbie Hancock (elp), Joe Zawinul (org), John McLaughlin (g), Dave Holland (b), Tony Williams (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: A leader date from the player who dramatically expanded the expressive range of the fretless bass. A groundbreaking record that established the bass as a solo instrument.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Jaco Pastorius (b), Herbie Hancock (p), Wayne Shorter (ss), Don Alias (perc), Narada Michael Walden / Lenny White (ds), Randy Brecker (tp)

jazz-fusion.note: The founding album of the group that built a distinctive fusion style on Metheny's translucent guitar tone and pastoral melodies.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Pat Metheny (g), Lyle Mays (kbds), Mark Egan (b), Dan Gottlieb (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: A leader date showcasing the electric bassist's dazzling virtuosity, joining funk groove with fusion's technical demands.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Stanley Clarke (b), George Duke (kbds), Icarus Johnson (g), Steve Gadd / Gerry Brown (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: A leader date from a drummer of overwhelming technique, balancing rock power with jazz complexity. A fusion classic.
jazz-fusion.personnel: Billy Cobham (ds), Tommy Bolin (g), Jan Hammer (kbds), Lee Sklar (b), Joe Farrell (sax)

jazz-fusion.note: An ambitious work from a keyboardist known for his diverse synthesizer palette, showing the fusion of funk and jazz-rock.
jazz-fusion.personnel: George Duke (kbds, vo), John Heard (b), Leon "Ndugu" Chancler (ds)

jazz-fusion.note: A defining work from the guitarist who fused blistering-speed picking with Latin vocabulary, symbolizing the technical-virtuoso ethos of the fusion era.

smooth-jazz.note: Featuring Bill Withers on the hit "Just the Two of Us," this album set the template for the smooth jazz direction to come.

smooth-jazz.note: A polished sound driven by electric piano and orchestration, laying the template for smooth jazz to come.
smooth-jazz.personnel: Bob James (kbds), Eric Gale (g), Gary King (b), Steve Gadd (ds)

smooth-jazz.note: The breakthrough album from a group known for catchy melodies and buoyant grooves, bridging fusion and smooth jazz.

smooth-jazz.note: An album from a player known for a sharp, soulful alto tone, bringing funk and pop sensibility into jazz.
smooth-jazz.personnel: David Sanborn (as), Marcus Miller (b), Steve Gadd / Buddy Williams (ds), Hiram Bullock (g)

smooth-jazz.personnel: Earl Klugh (g), with a session rhythm section including Ronnie Foster (kbds)

smooth-jazz.note: The debut of a supergroup of top-tier session musicians. A leading example of smooth jazz balancing technical skill and accessibility.
smooth-jazz.personnel: Bob James (kbds), Lee Ritenour (g), Nathan East (b), Harvey Mason (ds)

smooth-jazz.note: An album from a saxophonist steeped in R&B groove sensibility. One of the commercial success stories of 1990s smooth jazz.

A debut from a player whose groove sense recalls R&B guitar traditions, showing new possibilities for guitar within smooth jazz.

smooth-jazz.note: The debut from a saxophonist with pop-friendly accessibility, one of the figures who fueled smooth jazz's 1990s boom.
A debut from a player skilled on saxophone and flute, marked by a sound that softly absorbs funk and R&B sensibilities.

acid-jazz.note: Sampled Blue Note masters and fused them with hip-hop beats. A record that bridged jazz and club music.
acid-jazz.personnel: Rahsaan & Kobie Powell (vo, MC), Geoff Wilkinson & Mel Simpson (prod, kbds). Uses samples including Herbie Hancock's "Cantaloupe Island."

acid-jazz.personnel: Ishmael Butler (Butterfly), Mary Ann Vieira (Ladybug Mecca), Craig Irving (Doodlebug) (vo, MC)

acid-jazz.note: A danceable work from a large New York club-scene collective, crossing Latin, funk, and jazz.

acid-jazz.note: A landmark work tightly binding jazz basslines to hip-hop beats, also notable for a guest appearance by Ron Carter.
acid-jazz.personnel: Q-Tip, Phife Dawg (vo, MC), Ali Shaheed Muhammad (DJ, prod). Ron Carter (b) guests.

acid-jazz.note: A groundbreaking project pairing live jazz musicians with rap. A defining work of the jazz-rap genre.

acid-jazz.note: The debut from a band that drove the UK acid jazz movement, modernizing the vocabulary of funk and soul jazz.

acid-jazz.note: The debut from a band blending 1970s funk with acid jazz sensibility, backed by real dance-floor strength.

acid-jazz.note: A work from a veteran of the UK jazz-funk scene, marked by polished grooves and an array of guest stars.
acid-jazz.personnel: Bluey (Jean-Paul Maunick) (g), leading a fluid lineup of musicians

acid-jazz.note: A work from a group at the roots of the UK acid jazz scene, distinguished by its fusion of poetic spoken word and jazz-funk.

acid-jazz.note: A defining work from the French artist who fused house music with jazz vocabulary, a crossover success spanning club and jazz worlds.

acid-jazz.note: An ambitious work from the Norwegian musician who fused electronics with jazz trumpet. A pioneering figure of nu jazz.

acid-jazz.note: A work from the German producer collective, weaving jazz samples with house beats through a DJ-honed sensibility.
acid-jazz.personnel: The Jazzanova collective (Alexander Barck, Jürgen von Knoblauch, and others) (prod)

acid-jazz.note: A work from a band that pursued live-instrument hip-hop, a pioneering example of bringing jazz improvisation into hip-hop's context.

acid-jazz.personnel: Ben Addison (ds), Simon Nelson-Smith (g), Richard Searle (kbds)
